text:
Let Builders Decide How Much Parking to Build

Somewhere in your city, a modest apartment building isn't getting built. The developer can't get financing, or the corner lot is too small, or the rents won't cover the cost. Often the culprit isn't zoning height limits or permitting fees. It's a line in the planning code that says every new unit must come with one and a half parking spaces, whether anyone wants them or not.

Cities should scrap minimum parking requirements. Not cap them, not trim them by a quarter, not grant waivers case by case. They should remove them, and let the people who build and finance buildings decide how much parking their tenants and customers actually need.

Start with what these rules are. Minimum parking requirements are mandates, usually written decades ago, that tie the number of off-street spaces to a building's use: so many per apartment, per thousand square feet of retail, per restaurant seat, sometimes per church pew. The numbers often trace back to surveys of suburban sites at peak demand, copied from one city's code to the next. The UCLA planner Donald Shoup, who spent a career studying them, described the process as closer to ritual than science. Few cities can explain where their ratios came from.

The rules are expensive. A space in a surface lot uses about 300 square feet of land once you count the aisles. A space in a structured garage can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and an underground space more still. Those costs don't disappear. They get folded into rents, mortgages, and the price of groceries and lunches, and everyone pays them, including people who don't own a car. In the United States, roughly one in ten households has no vehicle, and they tend to be poorer than average. Parking mandates make them subsidize the driving of their wealthier neighbours.

The rules also decide what gets built and where. On a small urban lot, the mandated garage can eat so much space that a project stops making sense. Developers respond by building fewer, larger, pricier units, or by not building at all. Many of the older neighbourhoods people now pay a premium to live in, with corner shops, apartments above storefronts, and buildings set right at the sidewalk, would be illegal to build under today's parking codes. When a city says it wants more housing and walkable main streets while keeping the rules that stop both, it is working against itself.

Then there is the land itself. Parking lots are dead zones. They pay little in property tax per acre, spread destinations apart so that walking and transit become impractical, and push cities outward. Mandated parking makes driving the default by making everything else harder, and then cites the resulting car dependence as proof that the parking was needed.

Removing the minimums does not ban parking. This is the most common misunderstanding. A grocery store in a car-oriented suburb will still build a lot, because its customers drive and its owners want their money. A residential developer will still include garages where buyers expect them, because units without parking would sell slowly. What changes is that the amount of parking follows real demand rather than a figure in a code book. Lenders, who are not known for recklessness, will make sure projects carry the parking their markets need.

We also have evidence now, not just theory. Buffalo, New York, dropped its citywide minimums in 2017. Minneapolis followed in 2021, alongside broader zoning reform, and saw housing production grow while rents stayed comparatively flat. California's AB 2097, passed in 2022, barred parking mandates near major transit across the state. In these places developers have kept building parking, just less of it and where it made sense, and small infill projects that never penciled out before are getting built.

The strongest objection is spillover: if new buildings bring cars without garages, residents will fight over curb space on neighbouring streets. That worry is real, but the fix lies in managing the curb, not in forcing every building to over-supply private spaces. Residential permit districts, meters priced to keep a few spaces open on each block, and better enforcement handle on-street demand directly. Free curb parking is a public asset that cities give away and then complain is scarce. Pricing it sensibly solves the shortage that minimums only shift around.

Others worry that removing mandates helps developers at residents' expense. The opposite is closer to the truth. Mandates are a hidden tax on housing, paid by renters and buyers. Removing them lowers the cost of producing a home, and in a supply-starved market, that matters more than almost anything else a city council can do for free.

Minimum parking requirements are a policy that costs money, uses land, raises rents, and works against nearly every goal cities claim to have on housing, climate, and walkable streets. They survive mainly out of habit. Cities should end them, manage their streets properly, and let buildings come with the parking people actually choose to pay for.
